questions.q: In the lab scenario, why does a second production instance turn out to be justified for the acquired subsidiary?
options: Because the subsidiary is a different legal entity, which alone is always enough to justify a second instance
Because the subsidiary's data-residency law requires certain data to physically stay within that country's infrastructure, and Domain Separation only partitions data logically, not physically
Because the subsidiary's team prefers managing its own instance
Because Domain Separation is incompatible with HR case management
questions.explain: Domain Separation partitions data logically within one instance's existing infrastructure region; it can't relocate physical storage, so a genuine residency law can require a separate regional instance.

questions.q: What would the recommendation be for a more typical acquisition with no data-residency constraint, per the lab's Step 2?
options: Still stand up a second production instance, since every acquisition is organizationally independent
Domain Separation inside the existing instance would almost certainly suffice, rather than a second production instance
No architecture decision is needed for a typical acquisition
Rebuild the parent's entire platform from scratch
questions.explain: Remove the residency constraint and Lesson 4's default applies cleanly: don't stand up a second instance just because it's a different legal entity.

questions.q: Inside the subsidiary's new regional instance, how should the scope boundary for its HR case management and incident process be decided?
options: By copying the parent company's existing scope exactly, regardless of ownership
By functional and ownership boundaries — since the subsidiary's own team builds, tests, and deploys this on its own release cadence, it gets its own scoped application(s)
Scope boundaries don't apply once a second instance exists
By assigning a new scope per individual table, with no regard to team ownership
questions.explain: The scope-boundary guidance from Lesson 6 still applies inside the new instance: a clean functional/ownership boundary justifies the subsidiary's own scoped application(s).

questions.q: How should the subsidiary consume shared ITSM logic the parent already built well, per the lab's recommendation?
options: By rebuilding that logic from scratch inside the subsidiary's own instance
By publishing the shared logic as its own versioned scoped application and pulling a specific pinned version, rather than always-latest
By granting the subsidiary direct database access to the parent's tables
Shared ITSM logic cannot be reused across separate instances at all
questions.explain: Publishing reusable logic as a versioned scoped application and pinning to a specific version avoids both duplicated rebuilding and breakage from an always-changing dependency.

questions.q: What is the correct order of architectural decisions this lab demonstrates?
options: Scope boundaries first, then Domain Separation, then instance strategy last
All three decisions are made simultaneously with no dependency between them
Instance strategy first (driven by constraints like data residency), Domain Separation second within each instance, and scope boundaries last based on team ownership
Domain Separation always comes first, regardless of any regulatory constraint
questions.explain: The residency law determines instance topology first because it can't be satisfied logically; only after that is settled do domain and scope questions get decided within each instance.
